questions.stem: Which Upanishad explicitly refers to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as the fifth Veda (pañcama-veda)?
stem_variants: In which Upanishad are Itihāsa and Purāṇa designated as the fifth Veda?
questions.answer: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
questions.explanation: Chāndogya Upaniṣad (7.1.2) specifically designates Purāṇas and Itihāsas as the fifth Veda alongside the four foundational Vedas.
questions.source_quote: The Chāndogya Upaniṣad also calls Purāṇas and Itihāsas the fifth Veda...

questions.stem: According to the Ādi Parva, out of the sixty lakh ślokas composed by Vyāsa, how many were allocated to the Pitṛs?
stem_variants: How many ślokas of Vyāsa's 60-lakh-śloka Mahābhārata were assigned to the realm of the Pitṛs?
questions.answer: 15 lakh ślokas
questions.explanation: Vyāsa's 60 lakh ślokas were divided as: 30 lakh for Devas, 15 lakh for Pitṛs, 14 lakh for Gandharvas, and 1 lakh for humankind.
questions.source_quote: 30 lakh for the Devas, 15 lakh for the Pitṛs, 14 lakh for the Gandharvas and 1 lakh for humankind.

questions.stem: In the Ādi Parva tree metaphor, which element represents the 'trunk' of the two respective trees?
stem_variants: Who constitute the trunks in the allegorical trees of Duryodhana and Yudhiṣṭhira?
options: Karṇa for the tree of anger, Arjuna for the tree of Dharma
Śakuni for the tree of anger, Bhīma for the tree of Dharma
Dhṛtarāṣṭra for the tree of anger, Kṛṣṇa for the tree of Dharma
Duḥśāsana for the tree of anger, Nakula-Sahadeva for the tree of Dharma
distractor_pool: Śakuni for the tree of anger, Bhīma for the tree of Dharma
Dhṛtarāṣṭra for the tree of anger, Kṛṣṇa for the tree of Dharma
Duḥśāsana for the tree of anger, Nakula-Sahadeva for the tree of Dharma
questions.answer: Karṇa for the tree of anger, Arjuna for the tree of Dharma
accepted_answers: Karṇa for the tree of anger, Arjuna for the tree of Dharma
questions.explanation: In Vyāsa's metaphor, Duryodhana's tree of anger has Karṇa as the trunk (Dhṛtarāṣṭra as roots, Śakuni as branches), whereas Yudhiṣṭhira's tree of Dharma has Arjuna as the trunk (Kṛṣṇa/Vedas as roots, Bhīma as branches).
questions.source_quote: Duryodhana is a huge tree of anger (Karṇa the trunk... while Yudhiṣṭhira is a tree of Dharma (Arjuna the trunk...

questions.stem: Why does the text state that classifying the Mahābhārata under Aristotle's definition of an 'epic' is a categorical blunder?
stem_variants: On what philosophical and structural ground is an Itihāsa fundamentally distinct from an Aristotelian epic?
options: An Aristotelian epic is constrained to a single incident with beginning, progress, and end, whereas an Itihāsa embeds universal instruction in the four Puruṣārthas across vast past events.
An epic must be entirely fictional poetry, whereas an Itihāsa is verified secular history based strictly on archaeological evidence.
An epic strictly avoids religious figures, whereas an Itihāsa deals only with mythic gods and rituals.
Aristotle required an epic to be written in dactylic hexameter, which cannot accommodate Sanskrit anuṣṭubh meters.
distractor_pool: An epic must be entirely fictional poetry, whereas an Itihāsa is verified secular history based strictly on archaeological evidence.
An epic strictly avoids religious figures, whereas an Itihāsa deals only with mythic gods and rituals.
Aristotle required an epic to be written in dactylic hexameter, which cannot accommodate Sanskrit anuṣṭubh meters.
questions.answer: An Aristotelian epic is constrained to a single incident with beginning, progress, and end, whereas an Itihāsa embeds universal instruction in the four Puruṣārthas across vast past events.
accepted_answers: An Aristotelian epic is constrained to a single incident with beginning, progress, and end, whereas an Itihāsa embeds universal instruction in the four Puruṣārthas across vast past events.
questions.explanation: An epic in Aristotle's conception focuses on one central episode with its origin, progress, and consequences. In contrast, an Itihāsa ('so indeed it was') provides an expansive pedagogical vehicle conveying instruction on the four Puruṣārthas.
questions.source_quote: Calling it an 'epic' is a categorical blunder, because it imposes the genre of one language on another. An Itihāsa narrates past events as stories that carry instruction on the four puruṣārthas.

questions.stem: What critical epistemological concern is expressed in Mahābhārata 1.1.205 regarding the Veda's relationship with the 'alpaśruta'?
stem_variants: Why does Mahābhārata 1.1.205 state that the Veda 'fears' the half-knowledgeable person (alpaśruta)?
options: The Veda fears injury and distortion by those of superficial learning who fail to interpret its profound mysteries through Itihāsa and Purāṇa.
The Veda fears being entirely replaced by the popular narratives of the Itihāsas among common householders.
The Veda fears that people of half-knowledge will memorize mantras without performing sacrificial rituals.
The Veda fears that strict grammatical study will eclipse devotional worship of the Avatāras.
distractor_pool: The Veda fears being entirely replaced by the popular narratives of the Itihāsas among common householders.
The Veda fears that people of half-knowledge will memorize mantras without performing sacrificial rituals.
The Veda fears that strict grammatical study will eclipse devotional worship of the Avatāras.
questions.answer: The Veda fears injury and distortion by those of superficial learning who fail to interpret its profound mysteries through Itihāsa and Purāṇa.
accepted_answers: The Veda fears injury and distortion by those of superficial learning who fail to interpret its profound mysteries through Itihāsa and Purāṇa.
questions.explanation: Mahābhārata 1.1.205 warns that the Veda fears the 'alpaśruta' (one with half-knowledge) who may misinterpret and harm it; therefore, Vedic truths must be elucidated and protected through the narratives of Itihāsa and Purāṇa.
questions.source_quote: Mahābhārata (1.1.205) also says the Veda fears the person of half-knowledge (alpaśruta), so Vedic meaning must be explained through Itihāsa and Purāṇa.
